title: Prove It: Agentic Cloud Investigation Series
content:
Event Report: “Prove It: Agentic Cloud Investigation Series” Event Information Organizers: CloudThinker × First Cloud AI Journey (FCAJ) Schedule: September 5, 12, and 19, 2026 · 09:00–12:00 Location: AWS Office, 26th Floor, Bitexco Financial Tower, 2 Hai Trieu Street, Saigon Ward, Ho Chi Minh City Role: Participant and member of Team HCM15 (Tyrex) Format: Three hands-on workshops using read-only AWS and Kubernetes demo environments Event Objectives Learn how to govern an AI Agent before granting it access to a cloud environment. Investigate cloud incidents by testing competing hypotheses and collecting traceable evidence. Practise working with AI Agents under explicit identities, permissions, guardrails, and operating boundaries. Build the ability to defend technical conclusions under time pressure. Produce three portfolio artifacts: Agentic Cloud Review, Incident Report, and Investigation Dossier. Program Principles The program emphasized evidence over confidence. Participants did not provide personal AWS credentials and did not modify infrastructure. The demo environments were read-only: teams could inspect, analyze, investigate, and recommend, but could not execute remediation.
Each session followed the structure LEARN → PRACTICE → SHARE, combining guided concepts, hands-on investigation, and presentation of findings.
Day 01 — GOVERN · Observe Before You Act Saturday, September 5, 2026
Main Activities Examined how the security boundary changes when an AI Agent receives access to a cloud environment. Identified the Agent identity and designed permissions according to the principle of least privilege. Defined operating boundaries and guardrails before granting access. Used a read-only Agent to review an AWS demo account without changing its resources. Recorded observations, risks, and recommended follow-up actions based on evidence. Outcome Understood why Agent governance must be designed before access is enabled. Distinguished read-only observation from permissions that can mutate resources. Practised supervising an Agent instead of automatically accepting its output. Completed the Agentic Cloud Review artifact and developed the Agent Supervisor skill. Reference: Day 01 — GOVERN
Day 02 — INVESTIGATE · From Signal to Root Cause Saturday, September 12, 2026
Main Activities Investigated a cloud environment that had been intentionally misconfigured. Challenged the Agent’s initial answer instead of accepting the first explanation. Developed competing hypotheses and tested them against evidence collected from the environment. Recorded claims, sources, and supporting or contradicting evidence in an Evidence Table. Constructed a Causal Graph connecting the observed symptoms to the underlying cause. Consolidated the investigation into an Incident Report. Outcome Improved the ability to distinguish observations, hypotheses, evidence, and conclusions. Practised rejecting unsupported claims and tracing each conclusion back to its source. Completed the Incident Report artifact and developed the Agentic Incident Investigator skill. Team HCM15 (Tyrex) achieved a score of 93.6/100 for the Day 02 submission. Reference: Day 02 — INVESTIGATE
Day 03 — OPERATE · Prove It Arena Saturday, September 19, 2026
Main Activities Competed in the Prove It Arena as a member of Team HCM15 (Tyrex). Received an unfamiliar cloud environment and performed a rapid initial review. Built an Environment Map covering the main resources, dependencies, access boundaries, and potential risks. Responded to an incident inject under time pressure. Divided responsibilities for Agent operation, competing-hypothesis review, evidence collection, causal analysis, and dossier preparation. Collected evidence with identifiable sources and timestamps, constructed a Causal Graph, and prepared the Investigation Dossier. Defended the team’s conclusions before the judging panel in the Final Defence. Outcome Applied the complete investigation workflow: rapid review, hypothesis development, evidence collection, causal reasoning, decision, and defence. Completed the Investigation Dossier artifact and practised the Agentic Cloud Operator skill. The Day 03 result was below the team’s expectations, revealing areas to improve in role assignment, time management, evidence verification, and technical defence. Reference: Day 03 — Prove It Arena
Arena Evaluation Rubric Agent governance and operating boundaries: 15 points Environment review and risk prioritization: 20 points Incident investigation and causal reasoning: 30 points Decision and remediation quality: 20 points Evidence defence and communication: 15 points Each hint incurred a two-point deduction, and claims without a traceable source received no credit. A conclusion of insufficient evidence could still receive credit when defended appropriately.
Overall Series Results Completed all three stages: GOVERN, INVESTIGATE, and OPERATE. Produced the three portfolio artifacts: Agentic Cloud Review, Incident Report, and Investigation Dossier. Developed the Agent Supervisor, Agentic Incident Investigator, and Agentic Cloud Operator skills. Based on the team’s combined performance across the three days, Team HCM15 (Tyrex) received the award “Most Impressive Submission from Ho Chi Minh City.” Key Takeaways An AI Agent must operate within a clearly defined identity, permission scope, and set of guardrails. The Agent’s first answer is a hypothesis, not a verified conclusion. Every important claim should be traceable to evidence and its source. Competing hypotheses reduce confirmation bias during incident investigation. Effective teamwork requires explicit roles for Agent operation, evidence recording, opposing hypotheses, causal analysis, and report preparation. A technically reasonable conclusion is not enough unless the team can communicate and defend it clearly. Event Experience The series provided a practical view of how AI Agents can support cloud operations without replacing human judgement. The most valuable lesson was to treat confidence as insufficient and require evidence before accepting a conclusion. Working with Team HCM15 (Tyrex) also highlighted the importance of role clarity, time management, and communication during an investigation.
Although the Day 03 performance did not meet the team’s expectations, the experience exposed concrete weaknesses that can be improved in future incident-response exercises. Completing the full series helped connect cloud governance, investigation, and operations into one evidence-driven workflow.

title: Event 2
content:
Report: “AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deep Dive Day 2” Purpose of the Event Overview of Agent Core Core components of an Agent: Memory, Observability, Evaluation, Policy & Security, Tools & Capability Supporting services such as Browser (web browsing/search), Code Interpreter (code execution environment), and Payment (payment integration) Hands-on Lab practice Speaker List Nghia Tran – Core components of an Agent Anh Pham – Hands-on Lab Key Highlights AI Agent Knowledge How context window sizing works, and Agent Core memory: understanding the context window limits of models (e.g., Claude can go up to 1 million tokens) to see why Memory is essential for storing and personalizing the user experience. Storage and retrieval mechanisms of Short-term & Long-term memory: Short-term memory stores raw messages synchronously to keep conversations coherent, while Long-term memory asynchronously extracts important information to store as vectors, using 4 main strategies: Summary, User Preference, Semantic, and Episodic. Memory partitioning via Namespace and access-control security: Using a Namespace structure (folder-like) to partition data for faster search and token savings. Security is established through IAM policies and fine-grained access-scoping mechanisms between agents. Pillars of Monitoring and Evaluation for Agentic AI Systems Observability: Operates on the philosophy “You cannot fix what you cannot see.” Integrates OpenTelemetry to collect data across 3 pillars: Logs (errors/system state), Traces (conversation flow), and Metrics (latency, token cost). Evaluation: Helps detect hallucinations and faulty reasoning that lead to incorrect tool calls. Provides 13 built-in evaluators running either On-demand (during development) or Online (real-time in production). Powerful Supporting Services (Capabilities) Cedar Policy & Security: Controls Agent behavior using the Cedar policy language (e.g., setting rules to auto-approve refunds under $100). Supports human-in-the-loop approval when thresholds are exceeded. Browser & Code Interpreter (Sandbox): Creates a safe simulated environment for the Agent to automatically browse the web/search for information and write/test code without affecting the user’s real system. Payment & Registry: Direct payment integration via Stripe/Coinbase. Sets up a Registry to register and reuse tools/APIs across departments within an organization. Agent Harness & Knowledge Base: Quickly bootstraps a minimal agent with just a model, system prompt, and tools. Connects RAG to an organization’s internal data (S3, SharePoint, OneDrive). Key Takeaways Design Thinking System Engineering mindset: Realizing that when building an AI Agent for a real enterprise, the core AI technology accounts for only 6%, while the remaining 93% is software engineering — memory handling, tool integration, monitoring, and security. Personalization & Responsibility: The importance of personalizing the user experience through long-term memory, while complying with sensitive customer data security rules and using AI responsibly. Technical Architecture Combining Memory sensibly: To optimize cost and avoid overflowing the context window, one needs to skillfully combine partial retrieval of short-term memory with key insights from long-term memory. Monitoring via AI Judge: Understanding how a mechanism that uses another intelligent AI model as a “referee” (LLM Judge) operates to evaluate each of the Agent’s reasoning steps against industry standards. Applications to My Work Applying Bedrock Agent Core Memory: Implementing a chat-history storage mechanism for the current project with retention configuration (e.g., keeping data for 7 days), partitioning customer data by Namespace to optimize token cost and improve search accuracy. Integrating AWS CloudWatch / Observability: Setting up monitoring metrics for latency and token consumption cost of each model to promptly adjust the system prompt. Experimenting with the Nova Micro model: Configuring simple tasks to switch from Claude to AWS’s new-generation Amazon Nova Micro model line to increase response speed and save on testing budget. Setting up a secure sandbox: Experimenting with integrating a simulated Code Interpreter to let the Agent automatically perform complex calculations or data analysis in isolation. Event Experience Attending the “AWS FCAJ Agent Forge - Deep Dive Day 2” workshop was a very rewarding experience, providing an extremely large amount of knowledge at an advanced level (L300 - Advanced). The speakers’ theoretical lectures helped the audience easily visualize how the system operates under the hood before the Agent Core tools automate and simplify it.
Learning from Highly Skilled Speakers The speakers from AWS shared their experience using the Kiro IDE with its file-steering mechanism to guide context, using UV to manage environments, and deploying AWS resources directly via the Agent Core CLI / CDK. Hands-on Technical Experience Explored the modular architecture of Amazon Bedrock Agent Core, which helped visualize how an Agentic AI system is decomposed into independent services for easier scaling and management. Learned how to set up and operate a multi-layer Memory system. Clearly distinguished between Short-term memory, which operates synchronously to maintain conversation flow, and Long-term memory, which operates asynchronously to extract long-term knowledge in vector form. Gained a deeper understanding of the Namespace structure (tree/folder format) used in long-term memory. This mechanism helps isolate the storage space of each actor/session and narrows the scope of similarity search, saving tokens and optimizing cost. Learned the system-monitoring approach through the 3 pillars of Observability (Logs, Traces, Metrics) based on the OpenTelemetry protocol. This helps visually measure latency, cost, and token consumption of each model. Applying Modern Tools Got hands-on with the AI-assisted code editor Kiro IDE, learning about the steering-document mechanism to quickly and accurately guide project context. Practiced using UV to manage and install dependencies in an isolated environment, along with Agent Core CLI and CDK to automate the packaging process and deploy resources to AWS via CloudFormation. Learned how to configure and switch the default model to the new-generation Amazon Nova Micro model line. This significantly increases response speed and maximizes cost savings during testing. Networking and Exchange An opportunity to connect and learn directly within the First Cloud and AI (FCAJ) community, gaining access to real-world deployment scenarios shared by experienced AWS Solution Architects in Vietnam. Gained a valuable real-world perspective from experts: in a real enterprise-grade Agentic AI system, the core AI technology accounts for only 6%, while the remaining 93% belongs to software engineering — memory handling, tool integration, monitoring, and security. Lessons Learned Building an AI Agent for an enterprise requires a rigorous multi-layered security mindset through detailed Access Scoping policies and the Cedar Policy language, in order to prevent sensitive data leakage between Agents. The Agent capability verification process (Evaluation), using 13 built-in evaluators split across 3 levels (Session, Trace, Span) combined with the LLM Judge mechanism, is a core solution for systematically detecting hallucinations before deploying a system to production. Migrating Agentic AI systems to serverless cloud platforms like Bedrock Agent Core helps organizations achieve high reliability in both Security and Scalability, at a cost optimized for actual usage volume. Photos from the Event Add your photos here Overall, this event provided not only technical knowledge but also helped me shift my mindset on application design, system modernization, and more effective cross-team collaboration.

title: Introduction
content:
VPC endpoints VPC endpoints are virtual devices. They are horizontally scaled, redundant, and highly available VPC components. They allow communication between your compute resources and AWS services without imposing availability risks. Compute resources running in VPC can access Amazon S3 using a Gateway endpoint. PrivateLink interface endpoints can be used by compute resources running in VPC or on-premises. Workshop overview In this workshop, you will use two VPCs.
“VPC Cloud” is for cloud resources such as a Gateway endpoint and an EC2 instance to test with. “VPC On-Prem” simulates an on-premises environment such as a factory or corporate datacenter. An EC2 instance running strongSwan VPN software has been deployed in “VPC On-prem” and automatically configured to establish a Site-to-Site VPN tunnel with AWS Transit Gateway. This VPN simulates connectivity from an on-premises location to the AWS cloud. To minimize costs, only one VPN instance is provisioned to support this workshop. When planning VPN connectivity for your production workloads, AWS recommends using multiple VPN devices for high availability.

title: Prepare the environment
content:
To prepare for this part of the workshop you will need to:
Deploying a CloudFormation stack Modifying a VPC route table. These components work together to simulate on-premises DNS forwarding and name resolution.
Deploy the CloudFormation stack The CloudFormation template will create additional services to support an on-premises simulation:
One Route 53 Private Hosted Zone that hosts Alias records for the PrivateLink S3 endpoint One Route 53 Inbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC Cloud” to resolve inbound DNS resolution requests to the Private Hosted Zone One Route 53 Outbound Resolver endpoint that enables “VPC On-prem” to forward DNS requests for S3 to “VPC Cloud” Click the following link to open the AWS CloudFormation console. The required template will be pre-loaded into the menu. Accept all default and click Create stack. It may take a few minutes for stack deployment to complete. You can continue with the next step without waiting for the deployemnt to finish.
Update on-premise private route table This workshop uses a strongSwan VPN running on an EC2 instance to simulate connectivty between an on-premises datacenter and the AWS cloud. Most of the required components are provisioned before your start. To finalize the VPN configuration, you will modify the “VPC On-prem” routing table to direct traffic destined for the cloud to the strongSwan VPN instance.
Open the Amazon EC2 console
Select the instance named infra-vpngw-test. From the Details tab, copy the Instance ID and paste this into your text editor
Navigate to the VPC menu by using the Search box at the top of the browser window.
Click on Route Tables, select the RT Private On-prem route table, select the Routes tab, and click Edit Routes.
Click Add route. Destination: your Cloud VPC cidr range Target: ID of your infra-vpngw-test instance (you saved in your editor at step 1) Click Save changes

title: Create an S3 Interface endpoint
content:
In this section you will create and test an S3 interface endpoint using the simulated on-premises environment deployed as part of this workshop.
Return to the Amazon VPC menu. In the navigation pane, choose Endpoints, then click Create Endpoint.
In Create endpoint console:
Name the interface endpoint In Service category, choose aws services In the Search box, type S3 and press Enter. Select the endpoint named com.amazonaws.us-east-1.s3. Ensure that the Type column indicates Interface. For VPC, select VPC Cloud from the drop-down. Make sure to choose “VPC Cloud” and not “VPC On-prem”
Expand Additional settings and ensure that Enable DNS name is not selected (we will use this in the next part of the workshop) Select 2 subnets in the following AZs: us-east-1a and us-east-1b For Security group, choose SGforS3Endpoint: Keep the default policy - full access and click Create endpoint Congratulation on successfully creating S3 interface endpoint. In the next step, we will test the interface endpoint.

title: Proposal
content:
⚠️ Note: The information below is for reference purposes only. Please do not copy verbatim for your report, including this warning.
In this section, you need to summarize the contents of the workshop that you plan to conduct.
IoT Weather Platform for Lab Research A Unified AWS Serverless Solution for Real-Time Weather Monitoring 1. Executive Summary The IoT Weather Platform is designed for the ITea Lab team in Ho Chi Minh City to enhance weather data collection and analysis. It supports up to 5 weather stations, with potential scalability to 10-15, utilizing Raspberry Pi edge devices with ESP32 sensors to transmit data via MQTT. The platform leverages AWS Serverless services to deliver real-time monitoring, predictive analytics, and cost efficiency, with access restricted to 5 lab members via Amazon Cognito.
2. Problem Statement What’s the Problem? Current weather stations require manual data collection, becoming unmanageable with multiple units. There is no centralized system for real-time data or analytics, and third-party platforms are costly and overly complex.
The Solution The platform uses AWS IoT Core to ingest MQTT data, AWS Lambda and API Gateway for processing, Amazon S3 for storage (including a data lake), and AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to extract, transform, and load data from the S3 data lake to another S3 bucket for analysis. AWS Amplify with Next.js provides the web interface, and Amazon Cognito ensures secure access. Similar to Thingsboard and CoreIoT, users can register new devices and manage connections, though this platform operates on a smaller scale and is designed for private use. Key features include real-time dashboards, trend analysis, and low operational costs.
Benefits and Return on Investment The solution establishes a foundational resource for lab members to develop a larger IoT platform, serving as a study resource, and provides a data foundation for AI enthusiasts for model training or analysis. It reduces manual reporting for each station via a centralized platform, simplifying management and maintenance, and improves data reliability. Monthly costs are $0.66 USD per the AWS Pricing Calculator, with a 12-month total of $7.92 USD. All IoT equipment costs are covered by the existing weather station setup, eliminating additional development expenses. The break-even period of 6-12 months is achieved through significant time savings from reduced manual work.
3. Solution Architecture The platform employs a serverless AWS architecture to manage data from 5 Raspberry Pi-based stations, scalable to 15. Data is ingested via AWS IoT Core, stored in an S3 data lake, and processed by AWS Glue Crawlers and ETL jobs to transform and load it into another S3 bucket for analysis. Lambda and API Gateway handle additional processing, while Amplify with Next.js hosts the dashboard, secured by Cognito. The architecture is detailed below:
AWS Services Used AWS IoT Core: Ingests MQTT data from 5 stations, scalable to 15. AWS Lambda: Processes data and triggers Glue jobs (two functions). Amazon API Gateway: Facilitates web app communication. Amazon S3: Stores raw data in a data lake and processed outputs (two buckets). AWS Glue: Crawlers catalog data, and ETL jobs transform and load it. AWS Amplify: Hosts the Next.js web interface. Amazon Cognito: Secures access for lab users. Component Design Edge Devices: Raspberry Pi collects and filters sensor data, sending it to IoT Core. Data Ingestion: AWS IoT Core receives MQTT messages from the edge devices. Data Storage: Raw data is stored in an S3 data lake; processed data is stored in another S3 bucket. Data Processing: AWS Glue Crawlers catalog the data, and ETL jobs transform it for analysis. Web Interface: AWS Amplify hosts a Next.js app for real-time dashboards and analytics. User Management: Amazon Cognito manages user access, allowing up to 5 active accounts. 4. Technical Implementation Implementation Phases This project has two parts—setting up weather edge stations and building the weather platform—each following 4 phases:
Build Theory and Draw Architecture: Research Raspberry Pi setup with ESP32 sensors and design the AWS serverless architecture (1 month pre-internship) Calculate Price and Check Practicality: Use AWS Pricing Calculator to estimate costs and adjust if needed (Month 1). Fix Architecture for Cost or Solution Fit: Tweak the design (e.g., optimize Lambda with Next.js) to stay cost-effective and usable (Month 2). Develop, Test, and Deploy: Code the Raspberry Pi setup, AWS services with CDK/SDK, and Next.js app, then test and release to production (Months 2-3). Technical Requirements
Weather Edge Station: Sensors (temperature, humidity, rainfall, wind speed), a microcontroller (ESP32), and a Raspberry Pi as the edge device. Raspberry Pi runs Raspbian, handles Docker for filtering, and sends 1 MB/day per station via MQTT over Wi-Fi. Weather Platform: Practical knowledge of AWS Amplify (hosting Next.js), Lambda (minimal use due to Next.js), AWS Glue (ETL), S3 (two buckets), IoT Core (gateway and rules), and Cognito (5 users). Hardware: $265 one-time (Raspberry Pi 5 and sensors). 7. Risk Assessment Risk Matrix Network Outages: Medium impact, medium probability. Sensor Failures: High impact, low probability. Cost Overruns: Medium impact, low probability. Mitigation Strategies Network: Local storage on Raspberry Pi with Docker. Sensors: Regular checks and spares. Cost: AWS budget alerts and optimization. Contingency Plans Revert to manual methods if AWS fails. Use CloudFormation for cost-related rollbacks. 8. title: Access S3 from on-premises
content:
Overview In this section, you will create an Interface endpoint to access Amazon S3 from a simulated on-premises environment. The Interface endpoint will allow you to route to Amazon S3 over a VPN connection from your simulated on-premises environment.
Why using Interface endpoint:
Gateway endpoints only work with resources running in the VPC where they are created. Interface endpoints work with resources running in VPC, and also resources running in on-premises environments. Connectivty from your on-premises environment to the cloud can be provided by AWS Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Interface endpoints allow you to connect to services powered by AWS PrivateLink. These services include some AWS services, services hosted by other AWS customers and partners in their own VPCs (referred to as PrivateLink Endpoint Services), and supported AWS Marketplace Partner services. For this workshop, we will focus on connecting to Amazon S3.

title: On-premises DNS Simulation
content:
AWS PrivateLink endpoints have a fixed IP address in each Availability Zone where they are deployed, for the life of the endpoint (until it is deleted). These IP addresses are attached to Elastic Network Interfaces (ENIs). AWS recommends using DNS to resolve the IP addresses for endpoints so that downstream applications use the latest IP addresses when ENIs are added to new AZs, or deleted over time.
In this section, you will create a forwarding rule to send DNS resolution requests from a simulated on-premises environment to a Route 53 Private Hosted Zone. This section leverages the infrastructure deployed by CloudFormation in the Prepare the environment section.
Create DNS Alias Records for the Interface endpoint Navigate to the Route 53 management console (Hosted Zones section). The CloudFormation template you deployed in the Prepare the environment section created this Private Hosted Zone. Click on the name of the Private Hosted Zone, s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com: Create a new record in the Private Hosted Zone: Record name and record type keep default options Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor (you saved when doing section 4.3) Click Add another record, and add a second record using the following values. Click Create records when finished to create both records. Record name: *. Record type: keep default value (type A) Alias Button: Click to enable Route traffic to: Alias to VPC Endpoint Region: US East (N. Virginia) [us-east-1] Choose endpoint: Paste the Regional VPC Endpoint DNS name from your text editor The new records appear in the Route 53 console:
Create a Resolver Forwarding Rule Route 53 Resolver Forwarding Rules allow you to forward DNS queries from your VPC to other sources for name resolution. Outside of a workshop environment, you might use this feature to forward DNS queries from your VPC to DNS servers running on-premises. In this section, you will simulate an on-premises conditional forwarder by creating a forwarding rule that forwards DNS queries for Amazon S3 to a Private Hosted Zone running in “VPC Cloud” in-order to resolve the PrivateLink interface endpoint regional DNS name.
From the Route 53 management console, click Inbound endpoints on the left side bar In the Inbound endpoints console, click the ID of the inbound endpoint Copy the two IP addresses listed to your text editor From the Route 53 menu, choose Resolver > Rules, and click Create rule: In the Create rule console: Name: myS3Rule Rule type: Forward Domain name: s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com VPC: VPC On-prem Outbound endpoint: VPCOnpremOutboundEndpoint Target IP Addresses: Enter both IP addresses from your text editor (inbound endpoint addresses) and then click Submit You have successfully created resolver forwarding rule.
Test the on-premises DNS Simulation Connect to Test-Interface-Endpoint EC2 instance with Session manager Test DNS resolution. The dig command will return the IP addresses assigned to the VPC Interface endpoint running in VPC Cloud (your IP’s will be different): dig +short s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com The IP addresses returned are the VPC endpoint IP addresses, NOT the Resolver IP addresses you pasted from your text editor. The IP addresses of the Resolver endpoint and the VPC endpoint look similar because they are all from the VPC Cloud CIDR block.
Navigate to the VPC menu (Endpoints section), select the S3 Interface endpoint. Click the Subnets tab and verify that the IP addresses returned by Dig match the VPC endpoint: Return to your shell and use the AWS CLI to test listing your S3 buckets: aws s3 ls --endpoint-url https://s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com Terminate your Session Manager session: In this section you created an Interface endpoint for Amazon S3. This endpoint can be reached from on-premises through Site-to-Site VPN or AWS Direct Connect. Route 53 Resolver outbound endpoints simulated forwarding DNS requests from on-premises to a Private Hosted Zone running the cloud. Route 53 inbound Endpoints recieved the resolution request and returned a response containing the IP addresses of the VPC interface endpoint. Using DNS to resolve the endpoint IP addresses provides high availability in-case of an Availability Zone outage.

title: VPC Endpoint Policies
content:
When you create an interface or gateway endpoint, you can attach an endpoint policy to it that controls access to the service to which you are connecting. A VPC endpoint policy is an IAM resource policy that you attach to an endpoint. If you do not attach a policy when you create an endpoint, AWS attaches a default policy for you that allows full access to the service through the endpoint.
You can create a policy that restricts access to specific S3 buckets only. This is useful if you only want certain S3 Buckets to be accessible through the endpoint.
In this section you will create a VPC endpoint policy that restricts access to the S3 bucket specified in the VPC endpoint policy.
Connect to an EC2 instance and verify connectivity to S3 Start a new AWS Session Manager session on the instance named Test-Gateway-Endpoint. From the session, verify that you can list the contents of the bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC: aws s3 ls s3://\<your-bucket-name\> The bucket contents include the two 1 GB files uploaded in earlier.
Create a new S3 bucket; follow the naming pattern you used in Part 1, but add a ‘-2’ to the name. Leave other fields as default and click create Successfully create bucket
Navigate to: Services > VPC > Endpoints, then select the Gateway VPC endpoint you created earlier. Click the Policy tab. Click Edit policy. The default policy allows access to all S3 Buckets through the VPC endpoint.
In Edit Policy console, copy & Paste the following policy, then replace yourbucketname-2 with your 2nd bucket name. This policy will allow access through the VPC endpoint to your new bucket, but not any other bucket in Amazon S3. Click Save to apply the policy. { "Id": "Policy1631305502445", "Version": "2012-10-17", "Statement": [ { "Sid": "Stmt1631305501021", "Action": "s3:*", "Effect": "Allow", "Resource": [ "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2", "arn:aws:s3:::yourbucketname-2/*" ], "Principal": "*" } ] } Successfully customize policy
From your session on the Test-Gateway-Endpoint instance, test access to the S3 bucket you created in Part 1: Access S3 from VPC aws s3 ls s3://<yourbucketname> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy:
Return to your home directory on your EC2 instance cd~ Create a file fallocate -l 1G test-bucket2.xyz Copy file to 2nd bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-2nd-bucket-name> This operation succeeds because it is permitted by the VPC endpoint policy.
Then we test access to the first bucket by copy the file to 1st bucket aws s3 cp test-bucket2.xyz s3://<your-1st-bucket-name> This command will return an error because access to this bucket is not permitted by your new VPC endpoint policy.
Part 3 Summary: In this section, you created a VPC endpoint policy for Amazon S3, and used the AWS CLI to test the policy. AWS CLI actions targeted to your original S3 bucket failed because you applied a policy that only allowed access to the second bucket you created. AWS CLI actions targeted for your second bucket succeeded because the policy allowed them. These policies can be useful in situations where you need to control access to resources through VPC endpoints.

title: Workshop
content:

Secure Hybrid Access to S3 using VPC Endpoints Overview AWS PrivateLink provides private connectivity to AWS services from VPCs and your on-premises networks, without exposing your traffic to the Public Internet.
In this lab, you will learn how to create, configure, and test VPC endpoints that enable your workloads to reach AWS services without traversing the Public Internet.
You will create two types of endpoints to access Amazon S3: a Gateway VPC endpoint, and an Interface VPC endpoint. These two types of VPC endpoints offer different benefits depending on if you are accessing Amazon S3 from the cloud or your on-premises location
Gateway - Create a gateway endpoint to send traffic to Amazon S3 or DynamoDB using private IP addresses.You route traffic from your VPC to the gateway endpoint using route tables. Interface - Create an interface endpoint to send traffic to endpoint services that use a Network Load Balancer to distribute traffic. Traffic destined for the endpoint service is resolved using DNS. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Mon - Learn serverless-computing concepts - Compare AWS Lambda with continuously running EC2 instances 17/08/2026 17/08/2026 https://aws.amazon.com/serverless/ Tue 18/08/2026 18/08/2026 Wed - Learn Lambda fundamentals: functions, runtime, handler, execution role, memory, timeout, environment variables, and logs 19/08/2026 19/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html Thu - Learn event-driven architecture and common Lambda triggers, including S3, EventBridge, and API Gateway 20/08/2026 20/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-services.html Fri - Create a simple Lambda function and test it with sample events - Inspect its CloudWatch logs and review basic Lambda pricing 21/08/2026 21/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/getting-started.html Week 8 Achievements: Explained the serverless execution model. Distinguished Lambda workloads from EC2 workloads. Understood Lambda runtime, handler, execution role, timeout, and environment variables. Identified common event sources for Lambda. Created and tested a basic Lambda function and inspected its logs.

title: Week 9 Worklog
content: Week 9 Objectives: Understand the difference between monitoring, logging, and auditing. Learn the fundamental roles of Amazon CloudWatch and AWS CloudTrail. Apply basic AWS cost-monitoring and resource-management practices. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Mon - Learn observability fundamentals: metrics, logs, events, dashboards, and alarms - Distinguish monitoring from auditing 24/08/2026 24/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/aws-caf-operations-perspective/observability.html Tue - Learn Amazon CloudWatch metrics, namespaces, dimensions, dashboards, and standard EC2 metrics 25/08/2026 25/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/WhatIsCloudWatch.html Wed - Learn CloudWatch Logs and alarms - Inspect log groups and understand how alarms notify users when thresholds are exceeded 26/08/2026 26/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html Thu - Learn AWS CloudTrail: event history, management events, and how API activity is recorded for auditing 27/08/2026 27/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-user-guide.html Fri - Learn AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer, resource tagging, and basic methods for identifying and removing unused resources 28/08/2026 28/08/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cost-management/latest/userguide/what-is-costmanagement.html Week 9 Achievements: Distinguished metrics, logs, events, monitoring, and auditing. Understood the basic capabilities of Amazon CloudWatch. Understood how CloudTrail records AWS API activities. Created or interpreted a basic monitoring alarm. Understood AWS Budgets, Cost Explorer, tagging, and basic cost-control practices.

title: Week 10 Worklog
content: Week 10 Objectives: Understand synchronous and asynchronous communication. Learn the roles of Amazon SNS and Amazon SQS. Understand how queues and topics help decouple applications. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Mon - Learn application-integration fundamentals: synchronous, asynchronous, tightly coupled, and loosely coupled communication 31/08/2026 31/08/2026 https://aws.amazon.com/application-integration/ Tue - Learn Amazon SQS concepts: queues, messages, producers, consumers, visibility timeout, retention period, and dead-letter queues 01/09/2026 01/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/welcome.html Wed - Compare SQS Standard and FIFO queues - Learn message ordering, deduplication, and common use cases 02/09/2026 02/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/standard-queues.html Thu - Learn Amazon SNS concepts: topics, publishers, subscribers, message filtering, and fan-out architecture 03/09/2026 03/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/welcome.html Fri - Compare SNS and SQS - Study how SNS and SQS can be combined to build a decoupled application 04/09/2026 04/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sns/latest/dg/sns-common-scenarios.html Sat - Participate in Day 01: GOVERN · Observe Before You Act of the CloudThinker × FCAJ Prove It series as Team HCM15 (Tyrex) - Learn how AI Agent access changes cloud security boundaries - Design identity, least-privilege permissions, operating boundaries, and guardrails before granting access - Use a read-only Agent to review an AWS demo account and record evidence-backed observations - Complete the Agentic Cloud Review artifact and practise the Agent Supervisor skill 05/09/2026 05/09/2026 https://docs.cloudthinker.io/learn/workshops/prove-it/day-03-prove-it-arena Week 10 Achievements: Distinguished synchronous from asynchronous communication. Understood the main components of Amazon SQS and Amazon SNS. Distinguished Standard queues from FIFO queues. Explained the publish/subscribe model. Understood how SNS and SQS decouple application components.

title: Week 11 Worklog
content: Week 11 Objectives: Understand the fundamentals of web APIs. Learn the main components of Amazon API Gateway. Understand how API Gateway, Lambda, and EventBridge support serverless applications. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Mon - Learn API fundamentals: client/server, HTTP methods, endpoint, request, response, headers, status codes, and JSON 07/09/2026 07/09/2026 https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/api/ Tue - Learn Amazon API Gateway: REST API, HTTP API, routes, methods, stages, deployment, and Lambda integration 08/09/2026 08/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html Wed 09/09/2026 09/09/2026 Thu - Learn basic API protection: IAM authorization, API keys, throttling, CORS, input validation, and CloudWatch logging 10/09/2026 10/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/security.html Fri - Learn Amazon EventBridge: event buses, events, rules, targets, and schedules - Distinguish EventBridge, SNS, and SQS 11/09/2026 11/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-what-is.html Sat - Participate in Day 02: INVESTIGATE · From Signal to Root Cause with Team HCM15 (Tyrex) - Investigate an intentionally misconfigured cloud environment and challenge the Agent’s initial answer - Develop competing hypotheses, verify claims with evidence, and trace conclusions to their sources - Build an Evidence Table and Causal Graph, then consolidate the findings into an Incident Report - Practise the Agentic Incident Investigator skill and achieve a score of 93.6/100 12/09/2026 12/09/2026 https://docs.cloudthinker.io/learn/workshops/prove-it/day-03-prove-it-arena Week 11 Achievements: Understood basic HTTP and API concepts. Identified the main components of API Gateway. Explained how API Gateway integrates with Lambda. Understood basic API protection and monitoring. Distinguished EventBridge, SNS, and SQS use cases.

title: Week 12 Worklog
content: Week 12 Objectives: Understand container fundamentals. Learn how container images are created and stored. Understand the roles of Amazon ECR, ECS, and Fargate. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Mon - Learn container fundamentals - Compare containers with virtual machines 14/09/2026 14/09/2026 https://aws.amazon.com/what-are-containers/ Tue - Learn Docker concepts: image, container, Dockerfile, registry, port mapping, volume, and environment variable 15/09/2026 15/09/2026 https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-concepts/the-basics/what-is-a-container/ Wed - Learn Amazon ECR: repositories, image tags, authentication, image push/pull, and image lifecycle policies 16/09/2026 16/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECR/latest/userguide/what-is-ecr.html Thu - Learn Amazon ECS: cluster, task definition, task, service, container instance, and desired count 17/09/2026 17/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/Welcome.html Fri - Learn AWS Fargate and compare ECS on EC2 with ECS on Fargate - Draw a basic containerized application architecture 18/09/2026 18/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/AWS_Fargate.html Sat - Compete in Day 03: OPERATE · Prove It Arena with Team HCM15 (Tyrex) - Perform a rapid review of an unfamiliar cloud environment and respond to an incident inject under time pressure - Divide team roles, build an Environment Map, test competing hypotheses, collect timestamped evidence, and construct a Causal Graph - Complete the Investigation Dossier and Final Defence while practising the Agentic Cloud Operator skill - The Day 03 result was below the team’s expectations, highlighting improvements needed in role assignment, time management, evidence verification, and defence - Based on the combined performance across all three days, receive the award Most Impressive Submission from Ho Chi Minh City 19/09/2026 19/09/2026 https://docs.cloudthinker.io/learn/workshops/prove-it/day-03-prove-it-arena Week 12 Achievements: Distinguished containers from virtual machines. Understood images, containers, Dockerfiles, and registries. Understood how Amazon ECR stores container images. Identified the main components of Amazon ECS. Distinguished ECS on EC2 from ECS on Fargate.

title: Week 13 Worklog
content: Week 13 Objectives: Understand Infrastructure as Code. Learn the fundamental structure and workflow of AWS CloudFormation. Consolidate the AWS services studied during the first three months. Tasks to be carried out this week: Day Task Start Date Completion Date Reference Material Mon - Learn Infrastructure as Code - Compare repeatable templates with manually creating resources in the AWS Console 21/09/2026 21/09/2026 https://aws.amazon.com/what-is/iac/ Tue 22/09/2026 22/09/2026 Wed - Learn CloudFormation fundamentals: template, resource, parameter, output, mapping, stack, and change set 23/09/2026 23/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html Thu - Learn the CloudFormation workflow: validate, create, update, detect failures, roll back, and delete a stack 24/09/2026 24/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/stacks.html Fri - Review the first three months - Design a basic AWS architecture connecting VPC, EC2 or Lambda, S3, a database, monitoring, and IAM 25/09/2026 25/09/2026 https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/framework/welcome.html Week 13 Achievements: Explained the benefits of Infrastructure as Code. Understood the main sections of a CloudFormation template. Understood the CloudFormation stack lifecycle. Connected the AWS services studied during the first three months into a basic architecture. Established the foundational knowledge required for the project phase.
